source_refs.note: Topic 12.2, printed pages 266-270: disc slip, spondylosis, sciatica, arthritis, osteoporosis, dislocation, sprain and first aid.

blocks.text: The skeletal system is susceptible to a wide range of disorders that can affect its structure and function, in any part of it: the bones, joints and connective tissues.

The intervertebral discs between the vertebrae act as shock absorbers and help in movement. A herniated or slipped disc occurs when the outer layer of an intervertebral disc tears or ruptures, causing the inner gel-like substance to leak out and press against nearby nerves or the spinal cord. It may be due to trauma, degenerative changes with ageing, or repetitive strain on the vertebral column. Its symptoms include pain, numbness and tingling in the affected area, weakness or loss of muscle function, and in severe cases bowel or bladder dysfunction.

blocks.alt: Left: the lower back from behind with the vertebral column; a box and red patch mark the lumbar vertebrae. Right: the enlarged box shows two vertebrae with a disc between them whose inner material bulges backward as a herniated disc and bends the nerve running behind it. Labels: Lumbar vertebrae, Vertebra, Herniated disc, Pressed nerve.

blocks.text: Spondylosis is the degeneration of the vertebrae, intervertebral discs, ligaments or cartilage of the vertebral column. It may result in the narrowing and fusion of the intervertebral discs and the development of bone outgrowths, which put pressure on the nerves or spinal cord. It is most common in the lower back (lumbar vertebrae) and neck (cervical vertebrae). Its most common cause is the natural degeneration of the intervertebral discs; it occurs with ageing, genetic factors, trauma, prolonged poor posture and obesity. Symptoms include back or neck pain, stiffness and a reduced range of motion.

blocks.alt: Two side views of five vertebrae with discs. Left, Normal Vertebral column: even discs between the vertebrae. Right, Spondylosis: bone outgrowths on the vertebral edges, a narrowed disc and a slipped disc bulging backward.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.12: Spondylosis (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.12).

blocks.text: Sciatica is the compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve, which starts from the lower back and goes down through the buttocks into each leg. It is often caused by a herniated or bulging disc pressing on the nerve; other causes include trauma, infection, inflammation and spondylosis. Symptoms include pain or discomfort in the lower back, buttocks, legs or feet, tingling or numbness in the legs or feet, and weakness or difficulty moving the legs or feet.

blocks.alt: Left: the lower body from behind with a sciatic nerve from the lower back down each leg and a red area of pain along one leg. Right top: a side view of the lumbar spine where a herniated disc compresses the sciatic nerve. Right bottom: a vertebra seen from above with a bulging disc pressing on a nerve root. Labels: Sciatic nerve, Area of pain, Herniated disc, Sciatic nerve compressed, Bulging disc.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.13: Sciatica and its causes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.13).

blocks.text: Arthritis includes different inflammatory conditions that affect the joints. The symptoms of all types include joint pain and stiffness; others may include redness, warmth and swelling in the affected joints. Osteoarthritis is the most common type: the articular cartilage at the ends of the bones in a joint gradually softens and disintegrates; it affects the knee, hip and intervertebral joints. Rheumatoid arthritis results from an autoimmune disorder in which the synovial membrane becomes inflamed; most commonly the wrist and hands are involved. Gouty arthritis (gout) occurs when uric acid builds up in the blood and forms crystals in the joints, causing inflammation; the joint most commonly affected is that of the big toe, but the knees, wrists and fingers may also be affected.

blocks.alt: Three panels. Osteoarthritis: a knee joint with thin, broken articular cartilage (degenerated cartilage). Rheumatoid arthritis: a knee joint with a thick red swollen synovial membrane (inflammation in synovial membrane). Gouty arthritis: a foot from above with a red swollen big-toe joint containing needle-like uric acid crystals.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.14: Types of arthritis (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.14).

blocks.text: Osteoporosis is a condition of weakened bones that are more prone to fractures and breaks; it occurs when bone density decreases, making the bones fragile and porous. Its causes include the natural decrease in bone mass with age, which is more pronounced in some individuals; in women, the drop in oestrogen after the menopause, which accelerates bone loss; a lack of calcium and vitamin D in the diet, since calcium is crucial for bone strength and vitamin D helps the body absorb it; a lack of weight-bearing exercise; certain treatments such as the long-term use of corticosteroids; and smoking and alcohol consumption.

blocks.alt: Two square samples of spongy bone taken from a lumbar vertebra marked on a side view of the spine: normal bone with many small spaces, and bone with osteoporosis with fewer, much larger spaces.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.15: Normal bone and osteoporosis (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.15).

blocks.text: Joints can suffer a variety of injuries that result in pain, swelling and reduced motion.

items: Dislocation: the bones of a joint are forced out of their normal positions, as a result of a sudden impact or trauma. A severe dislocation can tear the muscles, ligaments and tendons; symptoms are swelling, intense pain and immobility of the joint. Rheumatoid arthritis can also cause dislocation. A dislocated joint can only be successfully corrected by a physiotherapist, and surgery may be needed to repair or tighten the stretched ligaments.

Sprain: an injury to the ligaments that connect the bones in a joint, most commonly in the ankle, knee and wrist. It happens when the joint is forced beyond its normal range of motion, stretching or tearing the ligaments; a foot turned inward tears the outer ligament, a foot turned outward the inner. Sprains are usually treated with physical therapy, and a dressing immobilises the sprain and provides support.

blocks.alt: Two rows. Normal elbow joint: a circle shows the humerus end fitting into the notch of the ulna with the radius beside it, next to a bent arm. Dislocated elbow joint: the ulna and radius are pushed back off the end of the humerus, and the arm beside it bulges at the back of the elbow. Labels: Humerus, Radius, Ulna.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.16: Dislocation in elbow joint (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.16).

blocks.alt: Two rows. Foot turned inward: a leg seen from the front with the foot rolled inward (arrow), and the ankle bones from the outer side with the outer ligament torn. Foot turned outward: the foot rolled outward, and the ankle bones from the inner side with the inner ligament torn.

blocks.text: First aid for dislocation and sprain

items: Immobilise the affected area: keep it immobile and do not attempt to realign the dislocated joint; use a sling or splint to support the limb.
Apply ice: an ice pack or cold compress on the affected area reduces swelling and pain.
Elevate the affected limb: in a dislocation, if possible, elevate the limb to help reduce swelling.
Seek medical attention: dislocations and sprains require medical attention, so call the emergency medical services on 1122 or take the person to hospital for further evaluation and treatment.
